analysis.one_liner: Speeds up repeal of the federal estate tax by three years, to 2007.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on July 25, 2001 and never received a vote before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2001 tax law (EGTRRA) had already scheduled the federal estate tax to phase out and be fully repealed in 2010. This bill would move that repeal up three years, to 2007, and drop the top tax rate on the largest taxable estates much faster — from 55% down to 9% by 2006. It would also speed up the cut in the maximum gift tax rate. The estate tax is paid only on transfers of very large estates, so the people who benefit from faster repeal are the heirs of the wealthiest families.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the largest estates — the small fraction of families whose inheritances are big enough to owe estate tax — gain the most, because their tax bill would drop to zero three years sooner and the top rate would fall to 9% almost immediately. Wealthy people planning large lifetime gifts would also pay less gift tax sooner. Estate planning itself would become simpler for those families, though professionals who make a living planning around the estate tax would lose that business.

how_it_helps.text: The bill moves the full repeal of the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes from 2010 up to 2007, amending the repeal dates throughout the tax code.
It accelerates the phasedown of the maximum estate tax rate so that the top rate falls to 45% in 2002 and reaches just 9% by 2006, instead of declining gradually to repeal.
It speeds up the reduction of the maximum gift tax rate to the top individual income tax rate, moving that change from 2010 to 2007.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury pays, in the form of revenue it would collect sooner under the existing schedule — and general taxpayers ultimately bear that, either through higher deficits or by making up the revenue elsewhere. The estate tax under the 2001 law already fell on a narrow group, so the savings concentrate almost entirely in the largest inheritances.

drawbacks.text: Faster repeal means the Treasury forgoes billions in tax that the existing 2001 law would have collected on very large estates between 2007 and 2010 — revenue that must be replaced through deficits or other taxes.

The benefit is concentrated: the estate tax applies only to transfers of the largest estates, so nearly all of the savings go to a small share of the wealthiest families rather than being spread across ordinary households.

Supporters' argument that repeal rescues family farms and small businesses was aimed at a group that owed little estate tax under the 2001 law's rising exemptions; the accelerating rate schedule in the bill text shows the deepest cuts going to the very top, not to modest estates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the narrow group of families with multi-million-dollar estates, the bill is a straightforward windfall: zero estate tax three years early and a near-zero top rate in the meantime. For everyone else, there is essentially no direct benefit and a shared cost in forgone revenue. The 2001 law had already delivered full repeal in 2010, so this bill's only real effect was to move up the date — a pure acceleration of an existing tax cut for the wealthiest inheritances.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Jennifer Dunn introduced the bill on July 25, 2001 and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
Eleven members cosponsored the bill — 9 of 223 House Republicans, 1 of 208 House Democrats, and the House's 1 Independent.
Ways and Means never reported the bill out, and no vote was ever scheduled in the House or Senate during the rest of the 107th Congress.
The 2001 tax law's existing schedule — gradual rate cuts leading to full estate tax repeal in 2010 — remained the law of the land, so nothing changed for estates as a result of this bill's failure.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Treasury kept the revenue it would have lost under the accelerated schedule, and estate planning professionals kept the business the tax generates. Heirs of large estates lost little, since the 2001 law's own repeal in 2010 remained on the books.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was nearly all Republican — 9 of 223 House Republicans and 1 of 208 House Democrats signed on — and the bill never reached a vote, so no recorded division beyond the cosponsor list exists.

industries.note: Accelerated repeal and a top rate of 9% by 2006 would eliminate taxes on the largest inheritances years early, concentrating the savings in families rich enough to owe the tax. The forgone revenue is a cost shared by all taxpayers.

industries.industry: Estate planning professionals (law firms and wealth advisors)
industries.note: Full, earlier repeal would shrink a client base built on planning around the estate tax. Their interest in keeping the tax runs against wealthy families' interest in repeal, though neither side maps cleanly onto ordinary people's.
